title: Making a gauge swatch
subtitle: Measuring stitches and rows over 10 cm
excerpt: Gauge is how many stitches and rows fit in 10 cm of your fabric. Checking it against the pattern before you start is what makes a hat fit and a blanket come out the planned size. This covers working a swatch, measuring it, and adjusting the hook.
sourceNotes: The 10 cm by 10 cm gauge swatch is a modern standard not named in Dillmont 1886, which sized work by stitch counts and thread grades. Reconstructed in our own words from the general principle of matching tension to a pattern, with the metric swatch convention drawn from the Craft Yarn Council standard gauge method.

glossaryTerms.definition: The number of stitches and rows that fit in 10 cm of crocheted fabric. Patterns state a target gauge so the finished piece comes out the planned size.
A small test square worked in the pattern stitch and the chosen yarn and hook, made to measure your gauge before starting the real piece.
Wetting or steaming a finished piece and letting it dry to shape. Because blocking can change the measurements, a swatch is often blocked before it is measured.

content.text: Your
gauge
is how many stitches and rows fit in 10 cm of your fabric. Two people working the same pattern in the same yarn can get different sizes because they crochet at different tensions. A quick
gauge swatch
before you start tells you whether your fabric matches the pattern, and lets you fix it before you commit hours to the wrong size.
What you need
The yarn and hook the pattern calls for, plus one size up and one size down for adjusting.
A soft tape measure or a rigid ruler.
Two pins to mark the measuring points.
How to do it
Work a square at least 15 cm across in the pattern stitch, so you have plain fabric well inside the edges to measure.
Block the swatch the way you will block the finished piece, then let it dry.
Lay it flat without stretching. Pin two points 10 cm apart across the middle.
Count the stitches between the pins, then count the rows over 10 cm the same way.
Compare both counts to the pattern. Too many stitches in 10 cm means your fabric is tight, so go up a hook size; too few means it is loose, so go down a size.
Work a fresh swatch with the new hook and measure again until the count matches.
You will know the gauge is right when the stitch count over 10 cm matches the pattern after blocking. Match stitches first; row count is easier to adjust by working a few more or fewer rows.
Common mistakes
Measuring a swatch that is too small, so the edges distort the count. Make it at least 15 cm and measure the middle.
Skipping the block. If the pattern is blocked, the swatch must be too, because blocking can change the count noticeably.
Stretching the swatch while measuring, which flatters the count and gives a piece that comes out too big.
When to use it

Always swatch for anything that has to fit or has to be a set size: garments, hats, and motifs that join into a planned blanket. You can skip it for free-form pieces where size does not matter, like a scarf you simply work until you run out of yarn. When in doubt, swatch, and block the swatch the way you will block the finished piece.
Blocking
changes the numbers more often than beginners expect.
